lesson.title: Burning Questions: Enthalpy of Combustion and Fuel Value
lesson.summary: The standard enthalpy of combustion is the heat released when exactly one mole of a substance burns completely in excess oxygen under standard conditions, and it is the quantity behind fuel energy ratings and food calorie values.
lesson.body:
Recall the general pattern of a combustion reaction: a fuel, usually a hydrocarbon, reacts with oxygen gas to produce carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy. The standard enthalpy of combustion, delta Hc degree, gives that general idea a precise definition: it is the enthalpy change when exactly one mole of a substance is burned completely in excess oxygen, under standard conditions, with the carbon fully oxidized to CO2(g) and the hydrogen fully oxidized to H2O(l) as a liquid. Combustion enthalpies are always negative, since complete combustion always releases energy.

This quantity has enormous practical importance well beyond the chemistry classroom. Fuel and energy industries rate different fuels partly by their enthalpy of combustion per gram or per mole, since a larger magnitude means more energy released per unit of fuel burned. Even nutrition labels trace back to this same idea: the Calorie content of food is historically determined by literally burning a sample of the food completely inside a bomb calorimeter and measuring the heat released, the exact same technique and the exact same device you met in the bomb calorimeter chapter.

As a worked example, use Hess's law with standard formation values to find the enthalpy of combustion of propane, C3H8(g) + 5 O2(g) results in 3 CO2(g) + 4 H2O(l), using delta Hf degree of C3H8(g) = negative 103.8 kJ/mol, delta Hf degree of CO2(g) = negative 393.5 kJ/mol, and delta Hf degree of H2O(l) = negative 285.8 kJ/mol. The products sum is (3)(negative 393.5) + (4)(negative 285.8) = negative 1,180.5 + negative 1,143.2 = negative 2,323.7 kJ. The reactants sum is (negative 103.8) + (5)(0) = negative 103.8 kJ. So delta H degree(comb) = negative 2,323.7 minus (negative 103.8) = negative 2,323.7 + 103.8 = negative 2,219.9 kJ/mol, meaning roughly 2,220 kJ is released for every mole of propane burned completely, a very energy dense reaction, consistent with propane's use as a fuel for grills, heaters, and portable stoves.

It is worth connecting this back explicitly to the bomb calorimeter, because that is almost always how a combustion enthalpy is actually measured in practice. A bomb calorimeter operates at constant volume and therefore measures delta U(combustion), not delta H(combustion) directly, exactly as you saw earlier. Converting from the measured delta U to the standard delta H degree requires a small correction, delta H = delta U + delta n(gas) R T, where delta n(gas) is the change in moles of gas between products and reactants, R is the gas constant, 8.314 times 10 to the negative 3 kJ/(mol times K), and T is the temperature in kelvin. For the propane reaction, the reactant side has 1 mole of C3H8(g) plus 5 moles of O2(g), 6 moles of gas total, while the product side has 3 moles of CO2(g) as gas (the water is liquid, so it does not count), so delta n(gas) = 3 minus 6 = negative 3. At standard temperature, T = 298 K, the correction term is delta n(gas) R T = (negative 3)(8.314 times 10 to the negative 3 kJ/(mol times K))(298 K) = negative 7.43 kJ/mol. Solving delta H = delta U + delta n(gas) R T for delta U gives delta U = delta H minus delta n(gas) R T = negative 2,219.9 minus (negative 7.43) = negative 2,212.5 kJ/mol. So a bomb calorimeter measuring propane combustion would report an internal energy change of about negative 2,212.5 kJ/mol, close to but not identical to the negative 2,219.9 kJ/mol standard enthalpy of combustion, a real difference of about 7.4 kJ out of roughly 2,220 kJ, or about three tenths of one percent. Small for propane, but this correction grows larger for reactions that involve a bigger change in moles of gas, which is exactly why chemists carefully distinguish delta U from delta H rather than treating a bomb calorimeter reading as the final answer.
